questions.text: In 'Edit note offline', what exactly gets written to the phone's SQLite: the note itself, an outbox row, or both? What does an outbox row contain?
questions.about: Phones keep notes in SQLite with an outbox

questions.text: What is the 'version' of a note, who increments it, and what does the phone send in a Push so the server can do the 'version check'?
questions.about: Conflicts are handled by version check

questions.text: When Phone B's Push gets 'Conflict', what exactly is the conflict copy: who creates it (server or phone), where does it live, and what happens to B's original edit and to the note A pushed?
questions.about: Conflicts are handled by version check and a conflict copy

questions.text: What is a change ID, who generates it, and what does the server do when it sees one it has already processed (what does it return)?
questions.about: Retries use change IDs

questions.text: What does 'Sent changes aren't edited' mean for a note the user edits again while its earlier change is still in the outbox or in flight?
questions.about: Sent changes aren't edited

questions.text: What is the cursor (a value from the change log?), who stores it, and when is it advanced during a paged Pull? What happens if a Pull fails halfway?
questions.about: A cursor tracks pull progress, paged

questions.text: What are the 'usual triggers' for sync, and does a Push always happen before a Pull?
questions.about: Sync is push plus pull, on the usual triggers

questions.text: What are the batching limits, and what happens to the outbox changes that don't fit in one Push? Also when does an outbox row get removed after 'Result'?
questions.about: Batching limits apply

answers.text: Both. The edit writes the note row and the outbox row in one SQLite transaction, so the UI and the queue never disagree. The outbox row holds the change ID, the note ID, the full note body and the base version, as the brief requires. The change ID is needed for safe retries. Reason: the brief says the phone queues the edit for upload, and that the queue carries the full body and starting version.

Each note has an integer version. Only the server sets it: it goes up by one on every accepted write. The phone stores the last server version it has seen for each note. A Push sends the full body and the base version, which is the server version the edit started from. The server accepts the change only if the base version equals the note's current version. Otherwise it is a conflict. Source: the brief's fixed requirements.

The server creates the conflict copy at the moment it rejects B's change. It is a new note with its own ID, at version 1, titled with the original title plus ' (conflict)', and it holds B's losing body. It lives on the server and enters the change log, so every device downloads it. B's original outbox change is removed once B gets the conflict result, and its text now lives only in the conflict note. The note A pushed is not changed. B's next pull replaces B's local copy with the winning version. Reason: the brief makes the server the source of truth and says the losing body is saved as a new note.

The phone generates the change ID (a unique ID) when it creates the outbox change, and every retry sends the same ID. The server records each processed change ID together with its result, in the same write as the change. When it sees an ID it has already processed, it returns the stored result and writes nothing. Reason: the phone cannot know whether a dropped request was applied, so the server must answer a repeat without applying it again. The brief does not fix the response format; this answer chooses the stored result.

Once a change has been sent, its body and change ID are never edited, so a retry sends exactly the same change. If the user edits the note again while the earlier change is in flight or still in the outbox: if the earlier change has not been sent, the edits collapse into it, as the brief requires. If it has been sent, the new edit becomes a new outbox change. It waits until the sent change has a result, then uses the version from that result as its base. Reason: otherwise its base version would be stale and it would conflict with the phone's own earlier edit.

The cursor is the sequence number of the last change-log entry the phone has applied. It is a value from the change log, as the brief implies. The phone stores it in its own SQLite database. During a paged pull, the phone applies one page of up to 500 entries and moves the cursor to that page's last sequence number in the same local transaction. If a pull fails halfway, the transaction does not commit, so the cursor does not move and the next pull reads the same page again. Re-applying an entry is harmless because an entry is applied only when its version is newer than the local one. Reason: this meets the brief's rule that an interrupted download must not cause a skipped or missed change.

The triggers are the ones the brief lists: the connection comes back, the app comes to the foreground, and every 60 seconds while online. Yes, a Push always happens before a Pull within one sync, because the brief says each sync uploads first, then downloads.

The limits are 100 changes per upload batch and 500 log entries per download page, both from the brief. Outbox changes that do not fit in one batch stay in the outbox. Reason: the brief does not say when they are sent. This answer sends the next batch in the same sync, until the outbox is empty or a batch fails, so a long offline session drains in one run instead of one batch per 60-second tick. An outbox row is removed only after the phone has a result for its change ID, either accepted or conflict. It is not removed when sent. If the result is lost, the row stays and is resent with the same change ID.

questions.text: When the phone gets an accepted result, does it update the note's stored version right away, or wait for the pull to bring the version in?
questions.about: Push: the server returns accepted with the new version

questions.text: If the sent change comes back as a conflict, what base version does the waiting new edit use, given the document says the conflict result has no version in it? What does that edit do then?
questions.about: Rules: the edit becomes a new outbox change and uses the version from that result as its base

questions.text: In this case, what does the phone do today when the pull applies the entry: does it overwrite the local body that the unsent change came from? What does the user see?
questions.about: Open questions: a pull brings a newer version of a note that still has an unsent change

questions.text: When a batch fails, what counts as a failure, and does the sync still go on to pull afterwards? When does the next sync try again?
questions.about: Push: until the outbox is empty or a batch fails

questions.text: When Phone B pulls, how does it end up with the conflict note, which it never had locally? Is a note it has not seen just inserted from the entry?
questions.about: Diagram: Pull after cursor, then Apply page in one transaction

answers.text: The phone sets the note's version to the accepted version at once, in the same local transaction that deletes the outbox change. Waiting for the pull would leave a waiting change with no base: the push runs before the pull in the same sync and needs that version now. Only the version is set, not the body.

A conflict result carries no version, so a waiting change keeps the base it already had. The server then sees that the base does not match and saves that body as a second conflict note. Nothing is merged or overwritten, and the server stays the only judge. Trade-off: one edit sequence can produce two conflict notes.

The brief does not say. As step 4 was written, the pull overwrites the local body, so the screen shows the server's text while the user's edit still sits in the outbox and becomes a conflict note on the next push. If the user edits that note again first, the new edit replaces the outbox body and the first edit's text is lost. The push drains the outbox before the pull, so this needs an edit made during the pull. I found no simple rule that avoids it without a new mechanism. Added to Open questions.

A batch fails when its request errors, times out, or the connection drops before all its results arrive. A conflict result is not a failure. On a failure the sync stops, does not pull, and the unanswered changes stay in the outbox. The next sync is the next trigger: the connection coming back, the app coming to the foreground, or the 60-second timer while online. Reason: a pull while the outbox still holds unsent changes leads to the case in Q11. The brief's upload-then-download order is kept; only the download is skipped when the upload fails.

Yes. Each log entry carries the full note (ID, title, body, version), so a phone with no row for that note inserts it from the entry. The brief says phones catch up by reading the log. A second fetch for new notes would add a request and a second cursor. The first version did not say that entries carry the note; the revised file now does.

questions.text: When the server saves a conflict note, what does a conflict note's own later life look like? If a phone edits it, does it get pushed with base version 1 like any other note?
questions.about: Conflict note: a new note the server creates from a losing edit

questions.text: The phone sets the note's version to the accepted version at once, but the pull later brings the same log entry for that note. Does the pull then do nothing for that note because the versions are equal? And what about the body when another phone's accepted write is newer?
questions.about: Step 3 Push, Accepted: it sets the note's version to the new version

questions.text: In a conflict, the phone's own note row still holds the losing body and the old version until the pull. What does the user see between the conflict result and the pull, and does the pull always run right after in the same sync?
questions.about: Conflict: it deletes the change

questions.text: When a phone first installs or has no cursor, what is the cursor's starting value, and does it pull the whole log from the beginning?
questions.about: Cursor: the sequence number of the last log entry the phone has applied

questions.text: The conflict case says the server 'adds log entries for it' (plural). Which entries are added, and does the existing note get a log entry on conflict even though it is unchanged?
questions.about: Step 3 Push, Otherwise it is a conflict

questions.text: How does a phone create a brand new note, and what base version does its first change carry? Is a new note covered by this document?
questions.about: Step 1 Edit

questions.text: If a sync is already running when another trigger fires (for example the 60-second timer), what happens? Can two syncs run at once?
questions.about: Step 2 Sync (triggers)

answers.text: A conflict note is created as a normal note at version 1 and is an ordinary note from then on. If a phone edits it, the change is pushed with its base version, which is the version the phone holds for it (1 after the pull), like any other note. Reason: the brief makes it a new note, and a special rule would add a mechanism the brief does not need.

Yes. The pull's entry for the phone's own accepted write has the same version, so the 'only if newer' rule changes nothing, and its body is the body the phone already sent. When another phone's accepted write is newer, the pull sets the title, body and version. That case is the first open question in the file.

The user sees the text they wrote until the pull replaces it. A conflict result is not a failure, so the same sync goes on to pull and the window is short. If the pull then fails, the window lasts until a later sync completes. The losing body is already saved on the server, so nothing is lost. The file now says this in step 3.

The cursor starts at 0, because sequence numbers start above 0 and 0 means no entry has been applied. The first pull reads the whole log in pages of 500. Reason: the brief says phones catch up by reading the log, and a new phone has no other source. The brief sets no limit on log size, so a very long log means a long first pull; I did not decide that here.

A conflict adds one log entry, for the conflict note, because the conflict note's creation is the one accepted write. The existing note is unchanged, so it gets no entry. The first version said 'entries', which was wrong, and the file now says one entry. The brief requires every accepted write to be in the log, and devices pick up the conflict note by downloading, which needs this entry.

Neither the brief nor the document says how a phone creates a new note, or what base version its first change carries. The document covers edits to notes the server already has. Added to Open questions.

Syncs do not overlap. A trigger that fires during a sync is skipped, and the 60-second timer sends any edit that missed it, at most 60 seconds later while online. Reason: two syncs at once would push and pull the same changes, which is hard to reason about. This is a rule about triggers, not a lock or lease, and the brief does not require more. Trade-off: a foreground trigger during a sync waits for the next timer tick.

teachbacks.text:
I'll follow one edit on Phone A to note N (server has it at version 1), from the tap to the point where the phone is caught up.

1. The user edits note N on Phone A. The edit starts the whole flow. The phone writes the new full body to the note row and writes a change to the outbox, both in one local SQLite transaction. The change holds a change ID the phone made, the note ID, the full body and the base version (1, the version the edit started from). The UI reads from SQLite, so it shows the new text at once, with no network call. State lives in the phone's SQLite. If the transaction fails to commit, nothing is written and the UI keeps the old text.
   - If N already has an unsent change in the outbox, the new edit replaces that change's body and keeps the original base version.
   - If N's change is already a sent change (its push has started but there is no result), the edit becomes a new outbox change and waits until the sent change has a result.

2. A sync starts. Three things can start one: the connection comes back, the app comes to the foreground, or a 60-second timer fires while online. A sync pushes first, then pulls. Syncs never overlap. A trigger that fires during a sync is skipped, and the 60-second timer sends any edit that missed it. If the push fails, the pull is skipped.

3. Push, phone side. The phone takes up to 100 unsent changes, oldest first. Each carries its change ID, full body and base version. It sends them to the server. The sent changes are never edited after this, so a retry sends exactly the same bytes and the same change ID.

4. Push, server side. The server handles the changes one at a time, in order. For each one it records the result under the change ID in the same write as the change itself. Server state is the notes with versions, the change log, and a table of processed change IDs with their results.
   - If it has already seen the change ID, it returns the stored result and writes nothing.
   - If the note's current version equals the change's base version, it is accepted. The server saves the body, raises the version by one (N goes from 1 to 2), appends a change-log entry with the full note, and returns "accepted" with the new version.
   - Otherwise it is a conflict. This is what Phone B hits if it pushes base 1 after A's write made N version 2. The server saves the losing body as a new note titled "<title> (conflict)" at version 1, adds one log entry for that new note, and leaves the existing note unchanged. It returns "conflict" with no version.

5. Push, phone handles each result. For each result the phone runs one local transaction. It deletes the change only when it has a result for that change ID.
   - Accepted: it sets the note's version to the new version (2) and deletes the change. It does not touch the body.
   - Conflict: it deletes the change and leaves the note row alone. The user still sees their own text until the pull replaces it.
   - If a waiting change exists, its base becomes the version from the accepted result. After a conflict there is no new version, so the waiting change keeps its old base. The server then decides it again, and it probably becomes a second conflict note.
   - If more changes are waiting, the phone sends the next batch in the same sync. This repeats until the outbox is empty or a batch fails.

6. Push failure. A batch fails if its request errors, times out, or the connection drops before all its results arrive. A conflict result is not a failure. On failure the sync stops and does not pull. Results already received stay applied, and unanswered changes stay in the outbox with the same change IDs. The next sync resends them. If the server had already processed one, it returns the stored result, so the change is applied once. If the server stopped partway through a batch, each change was recorded on its own, so the phone resends the whole batch and the processed ones return stored results.

7. Pull. This starts only when the push finished with no failure. The phone asks the server for log entries after its cursor, which is the sequence number of the last entry it applied. It starts at 0, so a brand new phone reads the whole log. The server returns up to 500 entries in sequence order, plus the last sequence number. Each entry has the full note, so no second fetch is needed.

8. Applying a page. The phone applies the page in one local transaction.
   - If it has no row for the note, it inserts the note from the entry. This is how Phone B gets the "(conflict)" note it never saw.
   - If it has the row, it overwrites title, body and version only when the entry's version is newer than the local one. An entry for a version it already has, such as its own accepted write, changes nothing. This is also how B's screen switches from its own text to the winning version 2.
   - The cursor moves to the page's last sequence number in the same transaction.
   Notes and the cursor live in phone SQLite.

9. Repeat and finish. The phone keeps pulling pages until one comes back empty. At that point the phone is caught up and the sync ends. If the connection drops during a page, nothing from that page is applied and the cursor does not move. The next pull reads the same page again. Applying a page twice changes nothing, so no change is skipped or missed.

10. Result for the two-phone example. Phone A's edit wins as version 2. Phone B's edit is kept on the server as a separate note named "<title> (conflict)" at version 1. Both phones end up with both notes after their pulls complete. If B's pull fails right after a conflict, B's screen keeps its own text and the server already holds the losing body. A later sync that completes its pull fixes the screen, and nothing is lost.

One more case, from the open questions. If a pull brings a newer version of a note that still has an unsent change, the pull overwrites the local body. The unsent edit stays in the outbox and becomes a conflict note on the next push. If the user edits that note again before that push, the new edit replaces the outbox body and the first text is lost. The document says this can only happen if the user edits during a pull.
gaps: How a phone creates a brand new note, and what base version its first change carries. The document says it covers only notes the server already has.
How a failing push that keeps failing is handled. There is no retry limit, backoff or user-visible error, so I can only say the next trigger tries again.

What the phone does when the server returns a conflict for a waiting change that has no new base version beyond looping forever. The document says only that it becomes another conflict note, not how a user resolves them.
What the pull does to a note that has an unsent change in the outbox beyond overwriting the body. The document lists this as an open question without a rule.
Whether the phone's cursor is stored per phone only or the server tracks it. The document says the cursor is on the phone, so I assume the server tracks nothing, but it never says so.
